why: Supports 16a: deprivation follows punishment; supports 22b's harvest-loss image of khusr.
Rival initial misrecognition then deprivation qualifies 16a's garden-loss reading.
Qatāda identifies the deprivation as loss of the garden, supporting 16a and 22b.
Names the lost garden's benefit, supporting 16a's deprivation and 22b's loss image.
Attributes lost fruit to excluding the poor, supporting 16a's cause and 22b's loss.
Reports recognition and lost fruit, supporting 16a's interpretation of deprivation.
Reports lost way then deprivation for excluding poor, supporting 16a and 22b.
Qatāda explains deprivation as requital, supporting 16a's loss and its cause.
Reports the shift from denial to recognizing deprivation, supporting 16a's reading.
Exegetes identify barred poor and lost fruit, supporting 16a and 22b.
Ibn ʿAbbās supplies the rival initial reading: they thought they had lost the way.
Supports 16a's sequence: mistaken way, then deprivation caused by barring the poor.
Explains deprivation as lost benefit for denying the needy their due.
Reports the rival first impression that the burned garden was another place.
Identifies lost yield and blessing after initial misrecognition, supporting 16a and 22b.
Qatāda reports their rival initial thought that they had taken the wrong road.
Links wrong conduct and punishment to lost fruit, supporting 16a and 22b.
Attributes the lost fruit to withholding from the poor, supporting 16a and 22b.
Reports misrecognition and deprivation as requital for intended miserliness, supporting 16a.
Explains deprivation as their mistaken confidence despite resolving to bar the poor.
Attributes their garden's loss to their actions, supporting 16a's deprivation and 22b.
Generalizes the verse: sin can deprive someone of provision already prepared.
Explains the admission of deprivation as consequence of wrongdoing, supporting 16a.
Names their wrongdoing as cause of losing the garden's good, supporting 16a.
Reports initial misdirection then punishment destroying bounty, supporting 16a and 22b.
Reads deprivation as betrayal rebounding on them, supporting 16a's cause and 22b's loss.
Reports recognition of the orchard and loss of its produce, supporting 16a and 22b.
Explains lost expected good as response to intent to deprive the poor.
General reflection on whether calamity prompts repentance or deepens disbelief.
Qatāda reports their initial rival thought that they had lost the road.
Ibn Jurayj explains deprivation as recognizing the garden's landmarks and misfortune.
Eschatological question about whether the garden owners are saved.
Links deprivation to wrongful intent after their initial misrecognition.
Explains their correction from misdirection to deprivation through wrongdoing.
Says their punishment deprives them beyond what they planned for the poor.
Explains بل as a shift from intended poor-deprivation to their total crop loss.
Explains explicit نحن as restricting who is truly deprived.
Links wrong conduct in harvesting to exclusion and lost crop, supporting 16a and 22b.
Chronological placement of Sūrat al-Qalam in revelation order.
Dispute about the sūrah's revelation sequence.
Story background about the garden owner's identity and reported location.
Supports 16a's account of discovery and loss of the garden's harvest.
Narrative background on the early account's omission of names and dates.
Reads the garden's punishment as the story's lesson and worldly warning.
Supports the loss reading: devastation first obscures the garden, then reveals it gone.
Reports the poor-exclusion cause of the lost harvest, supporting 16a and 22b.
Offers a broader harvest application and rival sense: rendered destitute.
General dating of the sūrah as early Makkan.
Report about which sūrah sections are Makkan or Madinan.
Identifies miserliness as the cause of the owners' harvest loss.
